chapter_summary:
Effective storage management is a cornerstone of system administration, ensuring data integrity, availability, and efficient utilization of disk space. On Red Hat Enterprise Linux, this begins with understanding how to prepare physical storage for use, which typically involves partitioning. For older systems or specific compatibility needs, the Master Boot Record (MBR) partitioning scheme is often used, managed by the `fdisk` utility. MBR supports up to four primary partitions or three primary and one extended partition, which can then contain multiple logical partitions. However, MBR has a limitation of 2TB per partition. For modern systems and larger disks, the GUID Partition Table (GPT) is the preferred standard, supporting virtually unlimited partitions and much larger disk sizes, up to 9.4 ZB. `gdisk` is the command-line tool for managing GPT partitions, providing a similar interactive interface to `fdisk`. When partitioning, you'll specify the start and end sectors or sizes for each partition, ensuring no overlap and allocating space according to your system's needs, such as separate partitions for `/boot`, `/`, `/home`, and swap space.

Once partitions are created, they are raw blocks of storage that need a file system to organize data. The `mkfs` command family is used for this purpose. For instance, `mkfs.ext4` creates an ext4 file system, known for its robustness and journaling capabilities, making it a good general-purpose choice. `mkfs.xfs` creates an XFS file system, which is highly scalable and performant, especially with large files and directories, and is the default file system for RHEL 7 and later. When creating a file system, you can specify options like block size or inode ratio, though for most cases, the defaults are sufficient. After creation, a file system must be mounted to a directory in the existing file system hierarchy to become accessible. The `mount` command temporarily attaches a file system to a specified mount point, for example, `mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/data`. To make this mount persistent across reboots, an entry must be added to the `/etc/fstab` file. This file contains a list of file systems that the system should mount automatically at boot time, specifying the device, mount point, file system type, mount options (like `defaults` or `noatime`), and dump/fsck order. Incorrect entries in `/etc/fstab` can prevent your system from booting, so always double-check your syntax and consider testing with `mount -a` after editing.

A more flexible approach to storage management, especially in dynamic environments, is Logical Volume Management (LVM). LVM provides an abstraction layer over physical disks, allowing you to pool storage from multiple physical devices into a single, flexible storage pool. This pool can then be divided into logical volumes, which behave like regular partitions but can be resized, moved, and snapshot much more easily. The LVM process starts with `pvcreate` to initialize physical volumes (PVs) from raw disks or partitions. These PVs are then combined into a volume group (VG) using `vgcreate`. A VG acts as a pool of storage from which logical volumes (LVs) are carved out using `lvcreate`. For example, `lvcreate -L 10G -n mydata_lv my_vg` creates a 10GB logical volume named `mydata_lv` within `my_vg`. Once an LV is created, you then create a file system on it, just like a regular partition, e.g., `mkfs.xfs /dev/my_vg/mydata_lv`, and mount it.

One of the most powerful features of LVM is the ability to extend logical volumes dynamically. If your application or data requires more space, you can use `lvextend` to increase the size of an existing logical volume. For example, `lvextend -L +5G /dev/my_vg/mydata_lv` adds 5GB to the logical volume. However, merely extending the logical volume isn't enough; the file system residing on it also needs to be resized to utilize the newly available space. For ext4 file systems, `resize2fs /dev/my_vg/mydata_lv` will expand the file system to fill the logical volume. For XFS file systems, the command is `xfs_growfs /mnt/mydata_lv` (note: `xfs_growfs` operates on the mount point, not the device directly). It's crucial to resize the file system after extending the logical volume; otherwise, the extra space remains unusable. Common mistakes include forgetting to update `/etc/fstab` after changing a mount point or device, or attempting to mount a file system before it's been created. Always ensure you have backups before performing any disk operations, as incorrect commands can lead to data loss. Safety dictates that you should always verify the device name (e.g., `/dev/sdb`) before executing partitioning or formatting commands, as targeting the wrong disk can be catastrophic.

screens.title: Managing Local Storage & File Systems
screens.subtitle: Partition disks, create file systems, mount persistently, and manage storage with LVM

narration.text: Today we will build a practical understanding of local storage on RHEL. You will see how low-level disks become usable partitions, how file systems like ext4 and XFS organize data, and how LVM adds a flexible layer so storage can grow without downtime. We start by learning the partitioning tools: fdisk for legacy MBR layouts and gdisk for modern GPT disks. Then we create file systems with mkfs utilities, mount them, and make mounts persistent with /etc/fstab. Finally we cover LVM: turning disks into physical volumes, pooling them into volume groups, carving logical volumes, and safely extending both the logical volume and the resident file system. These skills matter because disk changes are irreversible without backups. Proper partitioning and using the right tool for disk sizes prevents boot issues and data loss. LVM helps when you outgrow a partition or need snapshots. As you progress, think of partitioning as carving the hard drive, file systems as the filing rules, and LVM as the storage workshop that lets you reshuffle drawers safely. Keep safety checks and device verification first. Ready to explore partitioning, filesystems, mounting, and LVM with clear, actionable steps and examples? Let’s begin.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Disk devices must be partitioned, formatted with a file system, mounted to a directory, and optionally managed through LVM for flexibility.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Managing Local Storage
16:9 HD Classroom

Managing Local Storage & File Systems

This lesson shows how to turn raw disks into usable storage for a Linux system. We'll cover partition schemes, creating ext4 and XFS file systems, mounting with /etc/fstab, and using LVM to build resizable volumes so your services can grow safely.

Partitioning
Choose MBR for legacy needs or GPT for modern large disks. Use fdisk or gdisk accordingly.
File Systems
Create ext4 for general use or XFS for large files and performance using mkfs utilities.
LVM
Combine disks into PVs, create VGs, carve LVs, and resize volumes without reformatting.
i
Explore Key Topics

Partitioning, file system creation, and LVM operations form a stepwise workflow you will practice in the hands-on lab later.

Concept Map
Partitioning
fdisk (MBR) or gdisk (GPT) to create partitions like /boot, /, and swap.
File Systems
mkfs.ext4 and mkfs.xfs produce organized storage on partitions or logical volumes.
LVM
pvcreate, vgcreate, lvcreate, lvextend — a flexible layer for growing storage.
Coming up
A step-by-step lab will show gdisk, mkfs.xfs, mount, /etc/fstab edits, and an LVM extension workflow using real commands.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you will master in this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to partition disks correctly, choose the right partition table for your disk size, create and configure file systems, and mount them so they persist after reboot. You will also learn the LVM workflow: initializing physical volumes, aggregating them into a volume group, creating logical volumes, and safely extending both the logical volume and the file system that sits on it. Each objective focuses on a practical, verifiable skill: using fdisk and gdisk to prepare storage devices, using mkfs commands to build ext4 or XFS file systems, editing and testing /etc/fstab entries so mounts survive reboots, and running pvcreate, vgcreate, lvcreate, lvextend, resize2fs, and xfs_growfs in the correct order. These are applied skills. For example, you will practice extending an XFS-backed web server data volume and confirming the increased capacity with df. You will also learn common mistakes to avoid, such as using an MBR tool on a 3TB disk, forgetting to create a mount point, or extending a logical volume without growing the file system. These checks protect systems from boot failures and data loss.

keyIdea.title: Objective set A
keyIdea.text: Prepare and use storage safely: partition, format, mount, and manage growth with LVM while preventing common mistakes.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Verification & Safety
screens.subtitle: Checks, commands, and common pitfalls to avoid

narration.text: This second objectives slide focuses on verification and safe operation. You will learn to confirm device names with commands that show block devices, to back up critical data before destructive operations, and to validate your /etc/fstab entries with mount -a. A key routine is to verify UUIDs for persistent mounts and to run fsck where appropriate before mounting. For LVM tasks you will also practice checking lvdisplay and vgdisplay to confirm sizes and free space before extending volumes. Safety matters because partitioning and formatting rewrite disk metadata. A single mistyped device name can destroy production data. We will cover simple habits to reduce risk: double-check device paths, create mount-point directories before editing fstab, run mount -a to test without rebooting, and prefer GPT for disks larger than 2TB. These verification steps are lightweight but prevent downtime. At the end of the chapter you should be able to list devices, check volume group free extents, and run a safe resize sequence that grows both the logical volume and the filesystem without losing data.

keyIdea.title: Objective set B
keyIdea.text: Adopt verification steps and safe commands like mount -a and lvdisplay to prevent destructive mistakes during storage operations.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Verification & Safety

Verification & Safety

Develop repeatable checks that protect data during partitioning, formatting, and resizing workflows.

Confirm devices and UUIDs
Use block listing and blkid to confirm the correct disk and its UUID before editing /etc/fstab or running mkfs.
Mnemonic: See it, then change it
Test fstab with mount -a
After updating /etc/fstab run mount -a to catch syntax errors without rebooting. Fix errors before a production restart.
Mnemonic: Test, then trust
Check LVM state before changes
Use vgdisplay and lvdisplay to see free extents and current sizes. Never extend without confirming available space.
Backups and cautious steps
Always snapshot or backup critical data before destructive operations. Small verification steps avoid large recovery work.

screens.title: MBR vs GPT: Choosing the right partition table
screens.subtitle: Understand limits, partition counts, and when to use fdisk or gdisk

narration.text: Partition tables determine how a disk's space is divided and how the system locates boot information. The older Master Boot Record, commonly managed with fdisk, supports up to four primary partitions or an extended partition that contains logical partitions. MBR has a practical limit of 2 terabytes per partition, which makes it unsuitable for larger disks. GPT, managed with gdisk, is the modern standard: it supports many more partitions and disks far larger than 2TB. Use GPT for modern servers and large data drives, and reserve MBR only for compatibility with older boot loaders or legacy appliances. A concrete example: if you receive a new 3TB disk for database backups, fdisk’s MBR layout cannot address the full capacity safely. Use gdisk to create a GPT partition table and then create the partition you need. A common misconception is that fdisk always works; it will accept changes but the partition may silently be limited by MBR addressing. Another pitfall is overlapping start and end sectors: always ensure you set sizes or sector offsets that do not overlap existing partitions. Your takeaway: prefer GPT for anything over 2TB and choose your tool — fdisk or gdisk — based on the partition table you intend to use. How will you verify the chosen table before creating partitions?

keyIdea.title: Partition table choice
keyIdea.text: Use gdisk/GPT for modern, large disks and fdisk/MBR for legacy compatibility; verify limits before formatting.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › MBR vs GPT
Core Concept
MBR and GPT compared
MBR is limited to 2TB and four primary partitions. GPT supports larger disks and many partitions and is the recommended modern format for new systems. Choose the correct tool: fdisk for MBR, gdisk for GPT.
Common mistakes
  • Using fdisk on a 3TB disk may produce partitions that cannot use full capacity.
  • Not checking existing partition start/end sectors can cause overlaps.
  • Forgetting to set the correct type flags for special partitions like BIOS boot or EFI.
Comparison
Visual summary
fdisk vs gdisk
MBR (fdisk)
Up to 4 primary partitions, 2TB limit, legacy boot compatibility, use when required by older systems.
Example: Small boot-only media or legacy appliances.
GPT (gdisk)
Supports many partitions and disks larger than 2TB, required for modern large-volume servers and new installations.
Example: Use gdisk on a 3TB backup disk to access full capacity.
Quick verification commands
sudo fdisk -l /dev/sdb
sudo gdisk -l /dev/sdb
sudo parted -l
These commands show the partition table type and sizes so you can confirm the correct tool before creating partitions.
Key Takeaway
Prefer GPT for disks over 2TB. Use fdisk only for MBR/legacy scenarios and always verify the table type before writing changes.

screens.title: Creating partitions with fdisk (MBR) — workflow
screens.subtitle: Interactive partition creation steps and safety checks

narration.text: fdisk is the classic interactive tool for MBR-style partitioning. The workflow is deliberate: list devices, choose the correct device, start fdisk, create partitions by specifying start and end sectors or sizes, write the partition table, then verify. A concrete example: on a legacy 500GB drive you might create a small /boot partition, a root partition, and a swap partition. Start by running a device listing command to confirm the device name, then start fdisk against that device. When creating partitions, use the default alignment unless you have specific performance or RAID needs. After writing the table, run partprobe or reboot, and then create filesystems on the new partitions with mkfs. A common misconception is that fdisk will automatically detect and convert between MBR and GPT; it will not. Use fdisk only when you intend to create an MBR table. Another trap is failing to double-check the device: formatting the wrong disk is irreversible. Your final checks are to verify partition sizes and types, then create the filesystem and mount it. Would you rather test fdisk operations on a disposable VM disk first to build confidence?

keyIdea.title: fdisk workflow
keyIdea.text: List devices, run fdisk on the correct disk, create partitions with proper sizes, write changes, then verify before formatting.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › fdisk Workflow
Definition
Using fdisk to create MBR partitions
fdisk is interactive. You will explicitly create partitions, set types, and write the table. Stop if unsure — do not write until you have verified the device and sizes.
Common mistake
Writing changes to the wrong device. Always verify with a device listing command first and consider using a VM test disk when learning.
Process
A safe fdisk sequence and verification:
# 1. List and confirm device
sudo lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,MOUNTPOINT

# 2. Start fdisk for /dev/sdb
sudo fdisk /dev/sdb

# 3. Inside fdisk: n (new), p (primary), select start/end, w (write)

# 4. Inform kernel and create filesystem
sudo partprobe /dev/sdb
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1
Use partprobe or reboot to make the kernel aware of partitions before formatting.
Example card
Example: create a 1GB /boot partition and leave the rest for root. After fdisk, run mkfs on each partition and mount to test access before adding fstab entries.

screens.title: Creating partitions with gdisk (GPT)
screens.subtitle: Modern partitioning for disks larger than 2TB and many partitions

narration.text: gdisk is the GPT counterpart to fdisk and is the right tool for modern large disks. The steps mirror fdisk: confirm the device, run gdisk, create partitions by specifying sizes or end sectors, and write the partition table. For example, when preparing a 3TB backup disk, use gdisk to create a single partition that spans the disk and set its type. After writing the table, use partprobe or re-scan to make the kernel notice partitions. Then create an XFS file system if you expect large files, or ext4 for general-purpose workloads. A common misconception is that GPT is always required; small disks still work with MBR, but GPT avoids the 2TB limit and is future-proof. Another mistake is forgetting to set an EFI partition for UEFI systems when creating bootable system disks. For data-only disks that will be mounted under /mnt or /srv, simply create the partition and format it. The takeaway is to choose gdisk for large disks, validate partition boundaries, and only write once you have double-checked the device and sizes. How will you record partition plans before modifying a production disk?

keyIdea.title: gdisk workflow
keyIdea.text: Use gdisk for GPT tables on modern disks, confirm devices, create partitions, write, and then format with mkfs.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › gdisk Workflow
Definition
gdisk for GPT partition tables
gdisk manages GPT tables and supports large disks. Use it when disks exceed 2TB or when you need many partitions.
Common oversight
Not creating the EFI partition on a UEFI system when partitioning a boot disk. Plan boot partitions separately from data partitions.
Process
A safe gdisk sequence and verification:
# 1. Confirm device
sudo lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,MOUNTPOINT

# 2. Start gdisk for /dev/sdb
sudo gdisk /dev/sdb

# 3. Inside gdisk: n (new), specify size or sector, t (type) if needed, w (write)

# 4. Inform kernel and format
sudo partprobe /dev/sdb
sudo mkfs.xfs /dev/sdb1
Choose mkfs.xfs for large-file workloads; mkfs.ext4 for general purpose use.
Example card
Example: On a 3TB disk create one GPT partition, format it as XFS for database backups, then mount it under /mnt/db_backups and add a persistent fstab entry.

screens.title: File systems: ext4 and XFS
screens.subtitle: When to use ext4 vs XFS and how to create them with mkfs

narration.text: A file system organizes files and metadata on a partition or block device. Two common choices on RHEL are ext4 and XFS. Ext4 is robust, journaling, and a solid general-purpose file system that works well for many installations. XFS is optimized for scalability and high performance with large files and directories, and it is the default for later RHEL releases. To create a file system, use the mkfs family: mkfs. ext4 for ext4 and mkfs. xfs for XFS. Typically defaults are acceptable, but options exist to tune block sizes or inode density for specialized workloads. Concrete example: if you provision a partition for a web server's static content with many small files, ext4 is a safe default. If you prepare a storage volume for streaming large media files or large database file stores, XFS often performs better. A common misconception is that XFS cannot be resized; in fact XFS can be grown online with xfs_growfs but cannot be shrunk easily. Always format the device only after double-checking that the correct device is targeted. Your takeaway: choose the filesystem to match expected workload characteristics and use mkfs commands to create it, then test mounting and file operations before relying on the volume in production.

keyIdea.title: File system choice
keyIdea.text: Create ext4 for general purposes and XFS for large-file, high-throughput workloads; use mkfs.ext4 and mkfs.xfs respectively.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › File Systems
Definition
ext4 and XFS characteristics
ext4 is a stable journaling filesystem for mixed workloads. XFS is designed for scalability and large files. Choose based on file sizes, performance needs, and whether you may need online growth capabilities.
Create ext4
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1
Create XFS
sudo mkfs.xfs /dev/sdb1
Example scenario
You provision a 2TB volume for media storage. Choose XFS for better handling of large files and run mkfs.xfs, then mount and confirm write/read performance under expected load.
Misconception: XFS cannot be grown — it can be grown online with xfs_growfs while mounted, but cannot be shrunk easily.
Key Takeaway
Format after verifying device, and pick ext4 for general use or XFS for large-file performance; test before production use.

screens.title: Mounting and /etc/fstab for persistent mounts
screens.subtitle: Attach file systems and ensure they persist safely across reboots

narration.text: Mounting makes a file system accessible by attaching it to a directory in the existing hierarchy. The mount command attaches a device temporarily, such as mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/data. To persist mounts across reboots, add an entry to /etc/fstab using a stable identifier such as the device UUID. First, get the UUID with blkid or lsblk -f, then create the mount point directory and add the fstab line specifying device or UUID, mount point, file system type, options, and fsck order. A concrete example: after creating an XFS filesystem on /dev/sdb1, you might run sudo blkid /dev/sdb1 to obtain its UUID, then add a line like UUID=... /mnt/db_backups xfs defaults 0 0 to /etc/fstab. A common mistake is editing fstab with a wrong UUID or missing mount point, causing mount failures at boot. Test fstab edits with mount -a to catch errors without rebooting. If an fstab entry is wrong and prevents booting, you can drop to emergency mode or boot from rescue media to fix the file. The takeaway: use UUIDs, test with mount -a, and keep a recovery plan. What fstab entry will you test first on a non-production host?

keyIdea.title: Persistent mounts
keyIdea.text: Use blkid to find UUIDs, add fstab entries, and test with mount -a to make mounts persistent and safe.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Mounts & fstab
Definition
Temporary vs persistent mounts
Use mount for immediate access; edit /etc/fstab for automatic mounts at boot. Use UUIDs to avoid device name reordering issues.
# Get the UUID
sudo blkid /dev/sdb1

# Temporary mount
sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/data

# fstab entry (example)
UUID=a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7890-1234-567890abcdef /mnt/db_backups xfs defaults 0 0
Example & test
After adding an fstab line, run sudo mount -a. If there are errors, mount -a will show them so you can correct the UUID or options before rebooting.
Misconception: device names like /dev/sdb1 are permanent — they can change with hardware changes or different boot ordering. Use UUIDs to avoid surprises.
Key Takeaway

Always confirm UUIDs, create mount points, test with mount -a, and keep a recovery path for boot-time mount failures.

screens.title: LVM fundamentals: PV, VG, LV
screens.subtitle: Understand the abstraction layers that make storage flexible

narration.text: Logical Volume Management abstracts raw disks into a flexible pool. It starts with a physical volume, which is a partition or whole disk initialized with pvcreate. Physical volumes are combined into a volume group, created with vgcreate, forming a pool of storage from which logical volumes are allocated with lvcreate. Logical volumes act like partitions but are easier to resize, snapshot, and move. For example, if you have /dev/sdb and /dev/sdc, you can pvcreate both, vgcreate a group named data_vg using those PVs, and then lvcreate a logical volume called data_lv of a chosen size. Then you build a filesystem on /dev/data_vg/data_lv just as you would on a partition. A common misconception is that LVM itself stores files — it doesn’t. LVM provides block devices that you format with a filesystem. Another pitfall is neglecting to check free extents in the VG before attempting to create or extend an LV. Always use vgdisplay and lvdisplay to confirm available space and the current logical volume layout. The core insight: LVM lets you pool devices and create resizable volumes so you can grow storage without repartitioning disks. How might you use LVM to simplify future capacity planning?

keyIdea.title: LVM layers
keyIdea.text: PV (physical) → VG (pool) → LV (virtual partition) — LVM provides flexible allocation and resizing of storage.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › LVM Fundamentals
Definition
PV, VG and LV explained
Physical Volumes are disks or partitions initialized for LVM. Volume Groups pool those PVs into free space. Logical Volumes are carved from VGs and formatted with file systems.
pvcreate
Initialize /dev/sdc as a physical volume so LVM can manage it.
vgcreate
Combine PVs into a volume group like vg_data, which provides a pool of extents.
lvcreate
Carve a logical volume from the VG, create a filesystem, and mount it just like a partition.
Example commands
sudo pvcreate /dev/sdc
sudo vgcreate vg_data /dev/sdc
sudo lvcreate -L 10G -n data_lv vg_data
sudo mkfs.xfs /dev/vg_data/data_lv
sudo mount /dev/vg_data/data_lv /mnt/data

screens.title: Creating LVM volumes: pvcreate, vgcreate, lvcreate
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step commands to build a flexible logical volume

narration.text: Building a logical volume involves three explicit steps. First initialize physical storage with pvcreate. This writes LVM metadata so the device can be pooled. Second, create a volume group with vgcreate using one or more PVs. The VG aggregates free extents that can be allocated to LVs. Third, create a logical volume with lvcreate, specifying the size and name. After these steps, create a filesystem on the logical volume with mkfs and mount it. For example, to make a 10 gigabyte LV named mydata_lv in vg_data, run lvcreate -L 10G -n mydata_lv vg_data, then mkfs. xfs /dev/vg_data/mydata_lv and mount it. A concrete example is adding a single new disk to a database host: pvcreate the new disk, vgextend the existing group or vgcreate a new one, then lvcreate as needed. A common misconception is that creating an LV alone makes it usable; you must also create a filesystem on the LV and mount it. Another pitfall is forgetting to check vgdisplay for free extents before requesting a size larger than available. The takeaway: follow the three-step LVM creation sequence, verify free space, and remember to format and mount the LV. Which step will you automate for your environment?

keyIdea.title: LVM creation steps
keyIdea.text: Initialize PVs, create a VG, carve LVs, then format and mount — always verify free space with vgdisplay before lvcreate.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Create LVM Volumes
Core Concept
Three primary commands
pvcreate, vgcreate, and lvcreate form the basic creation sequence. Run them in order, then format and mount the new logical volume like any other block device.
Verification
Use pvdisplay, vgdisplay, and lvdisplay to confirm state and sizing before and after changes to avoid allocation errors.
Commands example
sudo pvcreate /dev/sdc
sudo vgcreate vg_data /dev/sdc
sudo lvcreate -L 10G -n mydata_lv vg_data
sudo mkfs.xfs /dev/vg_data/mydata_lv
sudo mount /dev/vg_data/mydata_lv /mnt/data
Remember to create the mount point directory before mounting and to confirm the LV path with lvdisplay.
Key Takeaway
Follow pvcreate → vgcreate → lvcreate, then mkfs and mount. Verify using display commands to avoid allocation and naming mistakes.

screens.title: Extending logical volumes and resizing file systems
screens.subtitle: Grow an LV with lvextend and expand ext4 or XFS filesystems safely

narration.text: When an application needs more storage, LVM lets you extend a logical volume without repartitioning. The sequence is: ensure the VG has free space, run lvextend to increase the logical volume size, and then expand the file system residing on that LV. For ext4, use resize2fs against the device path; for XFS, use xfs_growfs against the mount point because xfs_growfs operates on the mounted filesystem. A practical example: to add 5 gigabytes to /dev/vg_web/lv_html, run lvextend -L +5G /dev/vg_web/lv_html, then sudo xfs_growfs /var/www/html if the filesystem is XFS. Finally verify the size with lvdisplay and df -h. A frequent error is assuming lvextend alone is enough; the filesystem must be resized too. Another pitfall is attempting to grow XFS while unmounted — xfs_growfs requires the filesystem to be mounted. If you run into insufficient VG space, add another PV to the VG with pvcreate and vgextend first. The takeaway is to follow the three-step grow pattern: confirm space, extend LV, then grow filesystem. How would you verify each step in your environment before and after the change? Extending logical volumes and resizing file systems means confirm vg space, lvextend to add extents, then resize the filesystem with resize2fs (ext4) or xfs_growfs (xfs) to use the new space.. In practical terms, grow an lv with lvextend and expand ext4 or xfs filesystems safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Grow sequence
keyIdea.text: Confirm VG space, lvextend to add extents, then resize the filesystem with resize2fs (ext4) or xfs_growfs (XFS) to use the new space.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Extend LV & Resize FS
Definition
Extending an LV and its filesystem
lvextend adds space to the LV. Filesystems must then be grown to use the space: resize2fs for ext4, xfs_growfs for XFS (mounted).
Common mistakes
  • Running lvextend but forgetting to resize the filesystem.
  • Attempting to shrink XFS — it is not supported without complex steps.
  • Extending without free VG space.
Commands example
# Add 5GB to LV
sudo lvextend -L +5G /dev/vg_web/lv_html

# If ext4
sudo resize2fs /dev/vg_web/lv_html

# If XFS (operate on mount point)
sudo xfs_growfs /var/www/html

# Verify
sudo lvdisplay /dev/vg_web/lv_html
df -h /var/www/html
Always confirm the filesystem type before choosing the resize command.
Key Takeaway
Extending storage is a two-stage operation: expand the LV, then expand the filesystem. Verify with lvdisplay and df.

screens.subtitle: pvcreate, vgextend, lvextend and xfs_growfs in a practical sequence

narration.text: In this hands-on scenario you will expand a web server’s data volume. The server has an XFS logical volume mounted at /var/www/html from /dev/vg_web/lv_html. You add a new disk, /dev/sdc, and need to add 5GB to lv_html. Step one is to turn /dev/sdc into an LVM physical volume with pvcreate. Step two is vgextend vg_web /dev/sdc to add the new PV into the existing volume group. Step three is lvextend -L +5G /dev/vg_web/lv_html which increases the logical volume allocation. Step four is running xfs_growfs on the mount point /var/www/html to grow the XFS filesystem while it remains mounted. Finish by verifying the new size using lvdisplay and df -h. A concrete command sequence is shown visually so you can copy it into a test environment. A misconception to avoid is running xfs_growfs on the device; XFS grows by mount point. Also ensure vgdisplay shows enough free extents before lvextend. Always back up data before production changes. After the steps, confirm file accessibility and free space. What verification commands will you run to confirm success in your environment? Hands-on scenario: Expanding a web server data LV means pvcreate → vgextend → lvextend → xfs_growfs (on mount point) → verify with lvdisplay and df -h.. In practical terms, pvcreate, vgextend, lvextend and xfs_growfs in a practical sequence. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Webserver Expansion Lab
Scenario
Expand /var/www/html by 5GB using a new disk
You added /dev/sdc. The LV is /dev/vg_web/lv_html (XFS). We'll pvcreate, vgextend, lvextend, then xfs_growfs on the mounted path.
Warnings
Verify device names and confirm vgdisplay shows free space. Back up critical content before making changes to production storage.
# 1. Initialize new disk as PV
sudo pvcreate /dev/sdc

# 2. Add PV to existing VG
sudo vgextend vg_web /dev/sdc

# 3. Add 5GB to the LV
sudo lvextend -L +5G /dev/vg_web/lv_html

# 4. Grow the XFS filesystem (on mount point)
sudo xfs_growfs /var/www/html

# 5. Verify
sudo lvdisplay /dev/vg_web/lv_html
df -h /var/www/html
Example verification
Check vgdisplay for Free PE before lvextend. After growth, lvdisplay shows the new LV size and df shows the filesystem size increased.

screens.title: Common pitfalls and recovery steps
screens.subtitle: Protect systems from boot failures and data loss

narration.text: Working with disks is high risk without disciplined checks. Common pitfalls include formatting the wrong device, adding an incorrect /etc/fstab entry that prevents boot, extending an LV but forgetting to resize the filesystem, and using an MBR tool on a disk that needs GPT. Recovering from these mistakes often requires booting from rescue media or using emergency mode, so prevention is critical. Practice habits that reduce risk: check device names with lsblk, use blkid to capture UUIDs for fstab entries, run mount -a to validate fstab edits before rebooting, and snapshot or backup critical data before operations. A practical recovery step for a bad fstab line is to boot to a rescue environment, mount the root filesystem read-write, and edit /etc/fstab to remove or fix the offending line. If a partition is accidentally overwritten, recovery becomes complex and may require specialist tools; prevention and backups are the reliable strategy. A misconception is that lvextend always preserves data — while it is non-destructive when used correctly, user mistakes around device names or filesystem operations can cause data loss. The takeaway: build a checklist for every disk operation that includes device verification, backups, and post-change validation. What will your checklist include for a critical server change?

keyIdea.title: Preventive checklist
keyIdea.text: Use lsblk and blkid, test fstab with mount -a, backup before changes, and confirm VG/LV free space before extending.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Pitfalls & Recovery
Common Pitfalls
  • Formatting the wrong device due to mis-identified /dev names.
  • Editing /etc/fstab with incorrect UUIDs or mount points and rebooting.
  • Extending LV but not growing the filesystem.
Recovery steps
If fstab breaks boot, use rescue mode to edit /etc/fstab. If a wrong device was formatted, restore from backup. If lvextend fails, check vgdisplay and free extents.
Safety Reminder
Back up before destructive operations. Test commands in a disposable VM first. Prevention is far easier than recovery.

narration.text: These are the core terms to carry forward. Partitioning divides a physical disk into sections you can format and mount. MBR is the legacy partition table with a 2TB limit; GPT is the modern table for larger disks and more partitions. A file system, like ext4 or XFS, organizes files and metadata on a partition or logical volume. Mount points are directories where file systems become accessible. /etc/fstab records persistent mounts and should use UUIDs to remain stable across device renames. Memorize these definitions and use them when planning storage changes. For example, always ask whether the disk needs GPT for size, choose a filesystem that matches file size and performance needs, and plan mount points that match your administration strategy. These concepts are foundational for safe, repeatable disk operations.

keyIdea.title: Core terms
keyIdea.text: Partitioning, MBR vs GPT, File System, Mount Point, /etc/fstab — know these to plan and execute storage tasks safely.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Key Concepts

Key Concepts

Partitioning
Dividing a disk into logical sections for filesystems or LVM.
MBR & GPT
MBR is legacy with limits; GPT is modern and supports large disks and many partitions.
File System
ext4 and XFS are common; choose by workload characteristics and growth needs.
Summary: Choose GPT for large disks, create a suitable filesystem, use UUIDs in fstab, and test before reboot. These habits prevent downtime.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 2
screens.subtitle: LVM terms, commands, and safety checks

narration.text: Remember the LVM building blocks and the commands that operate them. A Physical Volume is initialized with pvcreate. A Volume Group is created with vgcreate and aggregates PVs into a pool. Logical Volumes are carved out with lvcreate and act as block devices that you format and mount. To grow storage, use lvextend and then resize the filesystem with resize2fs for ext4 or xfs_growfs applied to the mount point for XFS. Always verify VG free extents with vgdisplay and test /etc/fstab edits with mount -a. Keep backups and verify device names to avoid destructive errors. These concepts let you plan storage that can grow as your services need more space, while keeping recovery options simple. Practice the commands in a test environment and build a checklist that includes device verification, fstab testing, and post-change validation with lvdisplay and df. Your final question: what verification steps will you include in your live runbook to keep storage operations safe?

keyIdea.title: LVM & Safety
keyIdea.text: pvcreate, vgcreate, lvcreate, lvextend, and filesystem growth must be paired with verification commands and backups to prevent data loss.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › LVM & Safety

Key Concepts

Physical Volume (PV)
A disk or partition initialized for LVM with pvcreate.
Volume Group (VG)
A pool of storage combining one or more PVs for flexible allocation.
Logical Volume (LV)
A virtual block device carved from a VG; formatted and mounted like a partition.
Summary: Use LVM to build flexible, resizable storage. Verify free space, back up data, and test fstab changes. These practices keep systems resilient as they grow.
